# Draft:Roman invasion of Caledonia (139–142)

Causes
The period after 130 witnessed considerable instability in Roman frontier policy in the north. Shortly after his accession, Emperor Antoninus Pius ordered the reoccupation of southern Scotland and the construction of a new frontier barrier between the Forth and the Clyde. Governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus was given the order to occupy the Caledonian lowlands and fulfill this task. These territories were inhabited by the Otadini, Selgovae, Damnonii and the Novantae. Urbicus, a native of Tiddis in modern-day Algeria, had been one of a few senior officers selected by Hadrian to put down the Bar Kokhba revolt, which had been crushed with colossal loss of life and suffering. Lollius himself was awarded the highest military decorations, the corona aurea (gold wreath) and the hasta pura for his role in this campaign.
Course
The march
The Roman army would have marched north from the fort at Birrens (Blatobulgium), likely utilizing one of the at least three Roman temporary camps identified at Middlebie Hill. Several factors make it plausible that one of these camps served as the main headquarters during the campaign against the Caledonians. First, Middlebie Hill's location, approximately  south of Burnswark Hill, positioned between the Roman fort of Birrens and the Iron Age hillfort, provided a strategic staging point. Second, the hill offered excellent all-round visibility for reconnaissance and command. Third, the camps' substantial size could accommodate a significant force. Meanwhile, the two smaller temporary camps at the foot of Burnswark Hill itself may have functioned as assault camps established for the final stage of the attack, likely housing a force of several thousand soldiers. Regarding the route of advance, the Roman Road (or a predecessor trackway) probably constituted the primary approach through the moderately hilly terrain intersected by streams, passing Burnswark to the west and south en route to the River Clyde. The viewshed analysis revealed that the Roman army's approach along this road would have been clearly visible to Burnswark's occupants, particularly once the forces had crested Middlebie Hill. This visibility suggests that the hillfort's defenders had advance warning and time to prepare before the Roman army arrived at their position.
In Burnswark, 139/140
Upon arriving at Burnswark, the Roman army split into two wings and established camps at the southern and northern bases of the hill. Historians suggest this attack happened in 139/140, as the starting event for Quintus Lollius Urbicus' campaigns in Caledonia.
The size of the South and North Camps, when compared with the dimensions of a temporary legion camp, suggests that the attacking force comprised several thousand soldiers, approximately 2,600 to 3,100 men. The diverse range of munitions recovered from the site, including lead slingshot (glandes), iron arrowheads, and stone ballista balls, indicates that the army consisted of multiple vexillations drawn from different unit types. The slingers and archers were most likely auxiliary troops, while the ballista balls strongly suggest legionary participation, as these artillery pieces were typically operated by legionary personnel. The legions involved were the VI Victrix from Caerleon (under Publius Mummius Sisenna Rutilianus), the II Augusta from York (under Aulus Claudius Charax) and the XX Valeria Victrix from Chester (under Gaius Curtius Justus). Infantry also formed part of this force, evidenced by a Roman spearhead recovered between the South Camp and the East Gate. Cavalry may have been present as well, though no direct archaeological evidence for their participation has yet been found.
By securing control of the critical freshwater springs, Agricola's Well to the south and the Unnamed Spring to the north, and since Burnswark Hill lacks natural water sources on its summit, the hillfort's occupants depended on these springs for drinking water. By seizing them, the Romans simultaneously denied water to the defenders while ensuring their own supply. These positions also provided excellent observation points and clear fields of fire toward the hill's military crest. However, both camp locations had a significant tactical disadvantage: they were overlooked by the superior height of Burnswark Hill. Defenders on the ramparts could observe all movement within the Roman camps, which had no cover or concealment from above. The Romans' willingness to establish camps in such exposed positions suggests two things: first, that the hillfort's defenders lacked effective long-range weapons capable of threatening troops in the camps, and second, that the Romans felt no need to conceal their activities.found.
This confidence mirrors Roman behavior documented at other sieges, where commanders showed little concern about being overlooked by enemy fortifications. Both camps were constructed simultaneously using upcast earth from their surrounding ditches, with their ramparts facing the hill built more substantially than their other defenses. Despite their irregular morphology, both clearly functioned as blocking positions securing the freshwater springs. Each camp's long axis was oriented to maximize observation and fire coverage of the hill, and the matching distribution of munitions across both camps and the hillfort confirms they were part of a single coordinated operation. The South Camp appears to have housed the main striking force, including the legionary vexillation with its artillery, as evidenced by three ballista platforms positioned outside the north rampart, each aligned with one of the hillfort's three southern approach routes. The concentration of slingshot and arrowheads on the southern side suggests that most of the auxiliary slingers and archers were also stationed in this camp.
The distribution of munitions suggests the main Roman assault originated from the South Camp, targeting the southern face of Burnswark. This tactical choice exploited the gentler southern slopes (14–20% gradient) and three natural approach routes. However, the munitions pattern also indicates a coordinated secondary assault from the North Camp, forcing defenders to split their forces across two fronts. The Romans likely deployed in standard battle formation with infantry in the center, slingers and archers on the flanks, and possibly cavalry on the wings to prevent escape. The missile barrage served as suppressing fire to clear the ramparts as infantry advanced. Concentrated munitions clusters at key defensive positions, particularly flanking the Main/West Gate and East Gate, reveal where the fiercest resistance occurred. The assault probably breached the defenses first at the Saddle gates, splitting the defenders between the eastern and western summits. Each group was then overwhelmed in turn, with the final resistance likely collapsing on the western summit.
Doubts
Early investigators interpreted the site as one of major conflict involving overwhelming force, seemingly confirmed by an unprecedented quantity of Roman missiles found there, unparalleled in Britain. The debate over Burnswark centers on whether it was a Roman training site or an actual siege. Arguments for training include the possibility of an abandoned hillfort, irregular camp design suggesting practice construction, long-term occupation structures, and the absence of circumvallation. Arguments for siege/assault include evidence of occupation during missile barrage, tactical camp positioning, lead shot found at other conflict sites, and the principle that siege works match defender strength. The evidence remains evenly balanced, with each argument having a plausible counter-argument, making definitive interpretation difficult. However, even the dating of this attack remains uncertain. While around 140 is the most widely considered option, alternative dates have been proposed. Some scholars suggest a reconquest around 158, while others situate the attack within a possible Brigantian revolt dated to 154–158, though the evidence for such a revolt is tenuous and largely circumstantial. Supporting evidence for activity around AD 158 comes from the Roman fort at Birrens (Blatobulgium), which may have been burned at this time, based on an inscription discovered at the site.
Other operations
In 142, the Roman fort of Birrens (Blatobulgium) was raided and captured by the Caledonians. Other sources place this event just before the siege of Burnswark. Nevertheless, it is assumed that the city was reconquered by the Romans, due to a Roman inscription of the Legio XXII Primigenia from Mainz and the VIII Augusta from Strasbourg, claiming victory. Another victory inscription was found in Corbridge, and is attributed to the Emperor himself, Antoninus Pius. In Kirkandrews upon Eden, instead, an altar commemorating a victory of the Legio VI Victrix under Lucius Junius Victorinus Flavius Caelianus was found.
